title: I/O Buses & Interfaces
summary: The physical highways between the CPU and its peripherals, and why the bus you plug a fast device into can quietly cap its performance.

slides.markdown:
A **bus** is the physical wiring that carries data between the CPU/memory and peripherals — storage, GPUs, network cards. Like a highway, what matters isn't just how fast one car can go, but how many lanes exist and how the traffic is organized: **bandwidth** (how much data per second) and **topology** (shared line vs dedicated point-to-point paths).

A device's own speed is only half the story — if the bus connecting it can't carry that much data, the bus becomes the ceiling regardless of how capable the device is.

**PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express)** is a **point-to-point** bus — each device gets its own dedicated link to the CPU/chipset rather than sharing one wire with everyone else, unlike older shared buses. Bandwidth scales along two independent axes: **lane count** (x1, x4, x8, x16 — more physical lanes, more parallel bandwidth) and **generation** (each PCIe generation roughly doubles bandwidth per lane over the last).

This is why a device's real-world bandwidth ceiling depends on *both* numbers together — a PCIe 4.0 x4 link and a PCIe 3.0 x8 link land in a similar bandwidth range despite looking different on paper.

**SATA** (~600 MB/s ceiling for SATA III) was built specifically for storage — HDDs and early SSDs — and is now the slower, legacy option once flash outgrew it, which is exactly why NVMe moved storage onto PCIe instead ([nvme-and-storage-protocols](nvme-and-storage-protocols)).

**USB** targets general-purpose external peripherals — keyboards, drives, hubs — trading some raw bandwidth for universal compatibility and hot-plugging convenience. Modern USB (3.2, USB4) has closed much of the gap with internal buses for external storage, but it still typically trails a native internal PCIe connection for the fastest drives.

A simplified view of a modern system shows the CPU and memory controller at the center, with PCIe lanes fanning out to whichever devices need bandwidth.

![A simplified system topology: CPU and memory controller at the center, PCIe lanes fanning out to a GPU, an NVMe SSD, and other peripherals](assets/system-io-topology.svg)

Lane allocation is a real, finite resource — a motherboard has a fixed total lane budget, and giving more lanes to one device (a GPU) genuinely means fewer are available elsewhere, which is why high-end systems advertise their total PCIe lane counts as a spec that matters.

assets.alt: A simplified system topology: CPU and memory controller at the center, PCIe lanes fanning out to a GPU, an NVMe SSD, and other peripherals

slides.markdown:
Each PCIe generation roughly doubles per-lane bandwidth, which is what unlocks each new wave of faster storage and GPUs.

| Generation | Per-lane bandwidth (approx, one direction) | x4 link (approx) |
|---|---|---|
| PCIe 3.0 | ~1 GB/s | ~4 GB/s |
| PCIe 4.0 | ~2 GB/s | ~8 GB/s |
| PCIe 5.0 | ~4 GB/s | ~16 GB/s |

An SSD rated for PCIe 4.0 speeds simply cannot exceed the PCIe 3.0 ceiling if it's plugged into (or negotiates down to) a PCIe 3.0 link — the generation of the *slot*, not just the device, sets the real cap.

It's easy to buy a fast NVMe SSD and assume it'll deliver its full rated bandwidth — only to plug it into a narrower or older-generation PCIe link (say, an x2 slot, or a PCIe 3.0 chipset lane shared with other devices) and get a fraction of the advertised speed.

This isn't a defective drive; it's the bus becoming the bottleneck instead of the flash. Checking a motherboard's actual lane allocation and generation per slot — not just "it has an M.2 slot" — is essential before assuming a fast drive will actually run fast.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: what a real x4 NVMe link tops out at
slides.subTitle: Overhead eats into the theoretical number
slides.markdown:
PCIe 4.0 runs at ~2 GB/s per lane in one direction; an x4 link therefore has a theoretical ceiling of ~8 GB/s. But that number is the raw signaling rate before protocol overhead.

```
raw per-lane rate (PCIe 4.0) = ~2.0 GB/s
x4 link theoretical           = ~8.0 GB/s
encoding + protocol overhead   = ~2-3% (128b/130b encoding on Gen3+)
realistic sustained throughput = ~7.5-7.8 GB/s
```

An advertised '8 GB/s SSD' realistically delivers a bit under that, and real-world benchmarks land lower still once you add controller overhead, queue depth effects, and thermal throttling on sustained writes. The gap between a spec sheet's headline number and a benchmark's measured number is rarely a lie — it's usually these layered, compounding overheads, each individually small.

slides.sectionTitle: Lane allocation is a shared, finite budget
slides.subTitle: Why adding a GPU can slow down your SSD
slides.markdown:
A CPU or chipset exposes a fixed total number of PCIe lanes — say 24 or 28 on a mainstream desktop platform. Every device (GPU, NVMe SSD, network card, extra M.2 slots) draws from that same shared pool, and the motherboard's slot wiring decides how they're split.

This is why a manual sometimes warns "populating the second M.2 slot drops the GPU to x8" — the platform doesn't have enough total lanes to give everything x16/x4 simultaneously, so installing one device silently reallocates lanes away from another. It's a real, easy-to-miss constraint: two components can each individually support full bandwidth, yet not simultaneously, because they're drawing from the same finite lane budget.

slides.sectionTitle: Beyond PCIe: CXL and coherent interconnects
slides.subTitle: The next step past a plain peripheral bus
slides.markdown:
PCIe treats every device as a peripheral: the CPU and the device don't share a coherent view of memory, so software has to explicitly manage what data lives where. **CXL (Compute Express Link)**, built on the PCIe physical layer, adds a coherency protocol on top — letting an accelerator or memory-expansion device participate in the same cache-coherent memory space as the CPU, instead of being a black box behind a bus.

This matters for a concrete reason: memory-pooling and disaggregation, where a data-center server borrows extra DRAM attached over CXL as if it were local memory. A plain PCIe device could never do this cleanly — coherence is exactly the missing piece PCIe never solved, because it was never designed to.
